articles.title: WaveWash: Clean, Repair, and Dedupe Audio Datasets Before ML Training
articles.excerpt: Training speech models (Whisper, TTS, voice cloning) often breaks down because of dirty audio data: clipping, DC offset, background noise, low SNR, and duplicate samples quietly inflating validation m…
articles.body: Training speech models (Whisper, TTS, voice cloning) often breaks down because of dirty audio data: clipping, DC offset, background noise, low SNR, and duplicate samples quietly inflating validation metrics. I built WaveWash to automate audio quality control and data prep so developers don't have to write one-off scripts or manually listen to thousands of audio files. What WaveWash Does Tuned Presets: Built-in profiles for ASR (Whisper), TTS, Speaker ID, and Music Generation. Safe Auto-Repairs: Corrects DC offset, mild clipping, and normalizes loudness (EBU R128). Automated Segregation: clean/ : Audio that passed all checks. _error/ : Rejected files categorized by reason ( low_snr/ , clipping/ , etc.). _duplicates/ : Exact and near-duplicates set aside (nothing is deleted).

articles.title: HAMT: persistent maps, sets and vectors for Perl
articles.excerpt: HAMT is a new CPAN distribution that gives Perl three persistent containers: HAMT::Map, HAMT::Set and HAMT::Vector. "Persistent" here means an update never changes the container you call it on. It ret…
articles.body: HAMT is a new CPAN distribution that gives Perl three persistent containers: HAMT::Map , HAMT::Set and HAMT::Vector . "Persistent" here means an update never changes the container you call it on. It returns a new one, and the old one stays exactly as it was. That sounds expensive. With a Perl hash it is: to keep the old version you copy/clone the whole hash, so one change to a 100,000 key hash costs 100,000 copies. HAMT makes the same change by building four or five small nodes, and the new version shares everything else with the old one. This is useful anywhere a program copies a hash or array only so it can change it safely. A quick tour Every update method returns a new container. The receiver never changes.

articles.body: O teste que decide se uma automação de atendimento está pronta para um caso real A condição que nunca foi verdadeira Um atendente automático de mensagens tinha uma tarefa simples: reconhecer de qual anúncio a pessoa tinha vindo e citar o assunto já na saudação. Testei uma vez, funcionou, segui para o próximo cliente. A condição que checava isso nunca foi verdadeira. Nenhuma vez. Todo contato que chegava de anúncio recebeu a mesma saudação genérica, desde o primeiro dia, e nenhum erro apareceu em lugar nenhum. O painel mostrava mensagens entregues, zero falha registrada. A automação simplesmente fazia menos do que prometia, em silêncio, até alguém ler o histórico inteiro e notar o padrão. Funcionalidade que falha em silêncio parece funcionar para sempre.

articles.body: Now you see them, now you don't. Scientists have discovered that some of the universe's most powerful explosions, hypernovas, may not happen at all. These explosions, known as hypernovas , were first proposed to explain unusual stars in the halo of our galaxy, the Milky Way , and in a neighboring dwarf galaxy. It was suggested that these stars could only form from the debris of an explosion 10 times more powerful than the 'average' supernovas . The team behind these new findings suggests that ordinary supernovas could actually account for these stars when the uneven or non-spherical way they fling out matter is considered. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond. Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions. Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 13, 1773: Astronomer Charles Messier discovers the Whirlpool Galaxy before we ever knew it was a galaxy
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the "Whirlpool Galaxy," also known as Messier 51, or M51. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the " Whirlpool Galaxy , " also known as Messier 51, or M51. Charles Messier was scanning the sky for objects that could confuse comet hunters when he catalogued the galaxy as M51. However, Messier wasn't able to see the spiral structure, and he didn't identify it as a galaxy. Seventy-two years later, another astronomer named William Parsons saw the whirlpool shape, but he thought it was a spiral nebula. Eventually, Edwin Hubble found out that M51 and other features like it were actually galaxies. Spiral galaxy M51 (NGC 5194), The Whirlpool Galaxy, displays its long arms which consist of stars and gas laced with dust arranged in long lanes, in this view from the Hubble Space Telescope.

articles.excerpt: The sophomore season of "Star Trek: Starfleet Academy" will warp back to the small screen in March 2027 when the limited series returns for its final season on Paramount+.
articles.body: NEW YORK — Set your phasers to back-to-school, space fans. Star Trek is going back to Starfleet Academy for season 2, and we finally have a release date. The sophomore season of " Star Trek: Starfleet Academy " will warp back to the small screen in March 2027 when the limited series returns for its final season on Paramount+ . The series, which follows a class of cadets balancing Starfleet classes, space adventures (and yes, some love) in the 32nd century, will return with its full cast and even add new faces, showrunners announced at a panel at New York Comic Con 2026 on Saturday (Oct. 10). "Season one is about letting go of who you were in the past to start again at Starfleet Academy," executive producer and co-showrunner Noga Landau said in the Star Trek panel.
